narrative:
The model predicted that you have a 61.9% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is above 50%, the admissions system automatically rejected your law school application.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors from your academic record. Your class ranking at the end of your third year was the strongest influence and pushed the prediction strongly toward failure. You placed in the bottom decile of your class, far below the average of roughly the sixth decile among students who were accepted. This low ranking signaled to the model a higher risk that you would struggle with the bar exam.

Your LSAT score worked in the opposite direction and was the second most important factor. At 41, your score sits noticeably above the 37.2 average of accepted students, giving the model some confidence that you could still pass. Unfortunately, this positive signal was not large enough to overcome the negative impact of your class standing.

Your first-year class ranking was the third most important factor and again pushed the prediction toward failure. Placing in the second decile, well below the sixth-decile average of accepted students, reinforced the pattern of academic struggle.

Taken together, the model concluded that your relatively low class rankings outweighed your stronger LSAT performance. To improve your chances, you should focus on raising your academic performance in any remaining coursework, consider retaking the LSAT if possible, or explore schools and programs with different admissions criteria that place less weight on early class rank.
